title: Moderate Prenatal Cadmium Exposure and Adverse Birth Outcomes: a Role for Sex-Specific Differences?
ehr_evidence: The sample was derived from the ALSPAC study, a population-based study investigating environmental and genetic influences on the health, behaviour, and development of children; whole blood samples were analysed for cadmium (n = 4191) and birth anthropometry and gestational age were collected by study staff/questionnaires.
summary: In a prospective birth-cohort (ALSPAC) of 4191 singleton livebirths, higher prenatal maternal blood cadmium was adversely associated with reduced birthweight and crown–heel length overall and with reduced birthweight, head circumference, and crown–heel length in girls but not boys.
key_findings: In adjusted regression models (Model 3), maternal blood Cd was adversely associated with birthweight (unstandardized B −62.7 g, 95% CI −107.0, −18.4) and crown–heel length (B −0.28 cm, 95% CI −0.48, −0.07) in the whole group.

On stratification by sex, maternal blood Cd was adversely associated with birthweight (B −87.1 g, 95% CI −144.8, −29.4), head circumference (B −0.22 cm, 95% CI −0.39, −0.04), and crown–heel length (B −0.44 cm, 95% CI −0.71, −0.18) in girls but not in boys, with a significant interaction term sex × maternal B-Cd for all anthropometric variables (P for interaction <0.001).
There was no evidence of an increased odds of low birthweight in adjusted logistic regression models.
Maternal B-Cd was not a strong mediator in the associations between smoking and birth outcomes.
In smokers there was evidence of a weak adverse association with birthweight, not evident in non-smokers.
captured_features: Maternal age, parity, education, pre-pregnancy BMI, height, alcohol intake, active and passive smoking
population: Pregnant women from the former Avon Health Authority with expected delivery dates April 1991–December 1992 (UK), with 4191 singleton livebirths analysed; prenatal exposure measured in the first half of pregnancy.
limitations: A large number of B-Cd values were below the limit of detection, making use of Cd as a continuous variable in linear models less robust.
Unable to adjust for other environmental pollutants such as polychlorinated biphenols, with likely residual confounding.
